hints.title: Separate the condition from the claim
hints.body: For each statement, write what a number must satisfy before the statement applies, and what it then claims.
hints.recap: A counterexample meets the condition but breaks the conclusion.
hints.pitfall: A false statement may still have an irrelevant proposed counterexample.
hints.pause: Decide how the given number could fit each statement.

recall.reminder: A counterexample meets the condition but breaks the conclusion.

hints.title: Check the number in each role
hints.body: For a statement about 10p2±1, solve for a possible p and check that it meets the stated restrictions. For the other statements, test the given number against their opening conditions.
hints.recap: “Both” fails if just one of its two claims fails.
hints.pitfall: Do not substitute the same number for every letter without checking what each letter represents.
hints.pause: Determine exactly which statements the supplied example disproves.

recall.reminder: A counterexample must meet the condition and fail the conclusion.

solution:
For statement 1, choose p=3. It is an odd prime, but 10p2+1=91=7×13 is composite. Thus the claim that both expressions are prime fails.

Statement 2 concerns numbers already known to be prime and greater than 5. Since 91 is composite, it is not an allowed counterexample to that statement.

Statement 3 says a multiple of 7 greater than 7 is not prime. The number 91 satisfies rather than contradicts this conclusion.

Statement 1 only: B.
knowledgePattern: Test a specific composite number against three logical claims
